shape.scope: PURE MATHEMATICS (all of Paper 1; Section A of Paper 2). Functions: domain and range, one-one functions and inverses (restricting a domain so that an inverse exists; the graph of f^{-1} as the reflection of f in y = x; the domain of f^{-1} is the range of f), composite functions and the condition for fg to exist, repeated composition (f^2, f^{2025}(x) by finding the pattern); NOT (fg)^{-1} = g^{-1}f^{-1}, NOT restricting a domain to make a composite exist. Graphs and transformations: sketching y = (ax+b)/(cx+d) and y = (ax^2+bx+c)/(dx+e) with their asymptotes (vertical, horizontal, oblique), intercepts, turning points and symmetry; y^2 = ax, x^2 = by, the ellipse x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1 and the hyperbolas x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1, y^2/b^2 - x^2/a^2 = 1; the transformations y = af(x), y = f(x) + a, y = f(x + a), y = f(ax) and combinations described as a SEQUENCE (order matters); the graphs of y = |f(x)|, y = f(|x|) and y = 1/f(x) from y = f(x); simple parametric curves and their sketches. Equations and inequalities: formulating an equation, a system of linear equations (solved on the graphing calculator) or an inequality from a situation; solving an equation exactly or numerically; inequalities f(x)/g(x) > 0 with linear or quadratic f and g by a sign test, never by cross-multiplying; the modulus and |x - a| < b <=> a - b < x < a + b, |x - a| > b <=> x < a - b or x > a + b; solving an inequality from a sketch, and a related inequality by a substitution (x -> |x|, x -> e^x) into one already solved. Sequences and series: a sequence as a function of n, the relation u_n = S_n - S_{n-1}, sequences given by a formula or by a recurrence u_{n+1} = f(u_n) (generating terms, a limit L satisfying L = f(L) when the sequence converges, the behaviour read from a graph or a table), sum and difference of two series, convergence of a series and the sum to infinity, arithmetic and geometric series (nth term, sum to n terms, the condition |r| < 1 for convergence, the sum to infinity), finance and other models built on them (savings with increasing deposits, a loan with monthly interest and repayments, a bouncing ball); NOT the method of differences (removed in the revised 9758 — never set a telescoping sum; a sum whose result is GIVEN may be used for a change of variable), NOT mathematical induction. Vectors: 2-D and 3-D vectors, position, displacement and direction vectors, magnitude, unit vectors, distance between points, collinearity, the ratio theorem (a point dividing a line in a given ratio, midpoints), the scalar product (angle between vectors, a . n-hat as a length of projection, perpendicularity), the vector product (area of a triangle or parallelogram, |a x n-hat| as a perpendicular distance, a normal to a plane); vector and cartesian equations of lines and of planes (r . n = d, r = a + lambda b + mu c, cartesian); the foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line or a plane and the distance, the reflection of a point in a line or a plane; the angle between two lines, a line and a plane, two planes; the relationship between two lines (intersecting, parallel, skew), a line and a plane (meets in a point, lies in it, parallel to it), two planes (the line of intersection); problems in a stated 3-D situation (an aircraft path, a pipeline under a plane of rock); NOT the shortest distance or common perpendicular between two skew lines, NOT triple products. Complex numbers: extending the number system, complex roots of a quadratic, conjugate roots of a polynomial equation with real coefficients (and using them to find unknown real coefficients or the remaining root), modulus, argument (principal, in (-pi, pi]) and conjugate, the four operations in cartesian form, equality of complex numbers (a pair of simultaneous equations in z and w solved by elimination or by comparing real and imaginary parts), the Argand diagram, the geometrical effect of conjugation, negation, addition, subtraction and multiplication by i (a rotation through a right angle); NOT polar or modulus-argument form, NOT exponential form r e^{i theta}, NOT de Moivre, NOT loci. Differentiation: the sign of f' and f'' read from and drawn on a graph, the graph of y = f'(x) from y = f(x), implicit and parametric differentiation, the nature of stationary points by the first or second derivative test, tangents and normals (including to implicit and parametric curves, and where a tangent meets the curve again or passes through a given point), maxima and minima in a modelled situation (an area, a volume, a cost) with the maximum shown to be one, connected rates of change (a bowl filling, a ladder, a shadow); NOT non-stationary points of inflexion, NOT the second derivative of a parametric curve. Maclaurin series: the standard series for (1+x)^n with rational n, e^x, sin x, cos x, ln(1+x) with their ranges of validity (all in MF26), the first terms of a series by repeated differentiation (also from a differential relation such as dy/dx = k e^x (1 + y^2), differentiating that relation again), by repeated implicit differentiation, or by multiplying and substituting standard series (e^x cos 2x, ln((1+x)/(1-x)), (1+x)^n with a non-integer n, tan^{-1}(sqrt 2 + x) via its derivatives), the series as an approximation (an integral estimated from its first terms, a value of pi or ln 2), small-angle approximations sin x ~ x, cos x ~ 1 - x^2/2, tan x ~ x; NOT the general term. Integration techniques: f'(x)[f(x)]^n (n = -1 included), f'(x) e^{f(x)}, sin^2 x, cos^2 x, tan^2 x and products of sines and cosines via the factor formulae, the four standard forms 1/(x^2 + a^2), 1/sqrt(a^2 - x^2), 1/(x^2 - a^2), 1/(a^2 - x^2) (results in MF26), partial fractions, integration by a GIVEN substitution (including a trigonometric one for sqrt(a^2 - x^2)), integration by parts (including ln x, x^2 e^x, e^x sin x by two rounds), a modulus integrand split at its zero; NOT reduction formulae. Definite integrals: the integral as a limit of a sum, area under and between curves and lines (regions below the x-axis, areas against the y-axis, a parametric curve via integral y (dx/dt) dt), volumes of revolution about the x-axis or the y-axis (a cartesian curve, a region between two curves, a spherical cap or a bowl), exact values by hand where asked and numerical values from the graphing calculator otherwise; NOT the volume of revolution of a parametric curve. Differential equations: general and particular solutions of dy/dx = f(x) g(y) by separating variables, including reducing an equation to that form by a GIVEN substitution, second-order equations of the form d^2y/dx^2 = f(x) or a first-order equation in v = dx/dt by direct integration, formulating an equation from a situation (rate of change proportional to the amount, rate in minus rate out, a logistic-type dP/dt = kP(N - P), Newton cooling, a falling parachutist), interpreting the solution and its long-term behaviour, sketching the solution curve. PROBABILITY AND STATISTICS (Section B of Paper 2 only). Probability and counting: the addition and multiplication principles, permutations and combinations, arrangements in a line or a circle with repetition and restrictions (identical objects, objects together, objects separated), selection of committees with conditions; addition and multiplication of probabilities, mutually exclusive and independent events (tested numerically), tables of outcomes, Venn diagrams, tree diagrams and counting methods for probabilities, conditional probability P(A|B) = P(A and B)/P(B), P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B), games with turns and geometric-series probabilities, probabilities in terms of an unknown n or p. Discrete random variables: a probability distribution from a table, expectation and variance from it, E(aX + b) and Var(aX + b); the binomial distribution B(n, p) as a model with its two conditions stated in context (independent trials, a constant probability), its mean np and variance np(1 - p), probabilities and cumulative probabilities from the graphing calculator, the most likely value, a binomial on top of a binomial (the number of days on which an event happens), the range of p from a modal value; NOT cumulative distribution functions, NOT the Poisson distribution (removed from 9758), NOT the geometric distribution, NOT the normal approximation to the binomial. Normal distribution: N(mu, sigma^2) as a model, the standard normal, probabilities and inverse probabilities from the graphing calculator, the symmetry of the curve (drawn with its main features), finding mu and/or sigma from one or two given probabilities (standardising and solving), E and Var of aX + b and of aX + bY with X and Y independent (the sum of n independent copies X_1 + ... + X_n against the multiple nX; the difference of two totals; a percentage reduction as a scaling), the mass exceeded by a given percentage; NOT the normal approximation to the binomial. Sampling: population and simple random sample, why and how a random sample is taken and what makes one unsuitable, the sample mean as a random variable with E(X-bar) = mu and Var(X-bar) = sigma^2/n, its distribution from a normal population, the Central Limit Theorem for a large sample from any population (n >= 30 as the rule of thumb), unbiased estimates of the population mean and variance from raw data or from summarised data (sum x and sum x^2, or sum (x - a) and sum (x - a)^2). Hypothesis testing: null and alternative hypotheses stated with the parameter defined, the test statistic, critical region and critical value, level of significance and p-value, a test of a population mean from a normal population with known variance or from a large sample (a z-test), one-tail and two-tail tests and the reason for the choice, the conclusion in the context of the question, the assumptions a test needs, the range of a significance level or of a variance consistent with a stated conclusion; NOT the terms Type I and Type II error, NOT a test of the difference of two means, NOT a t-test. Correlation and linear regression: a scatter diagram and what it shows, the product moment correlation coefficient as a measure of linear fit and its interpretation (values near -1, 0 and 1; unaffected by a change of units), the least-squares regression line (the meaning of the residuals and of least squares; y on x, and x on y, and which to use), interpolation and extrapolation and the reliability of an estimate, a square, reciprocal, logarithmic or other transformation to achieve linearity and the choice between candidate models by comparing r; NOT deriving the formulae, NOT r^2 = b_1 b_2, NOT hypothesis tests on r. ASSUMED KNOWLEDGE (O-Level A Math): quadratics and the discriminant, surds, polynomials and partial fractions, binomial theorem for a positive integer index, indices and logarithms, trigonometric identities and the R-formula, the sine and cosine rules, basic differentiation and integration.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks (9758)
- Plain, exact, economical English. Every part is an imperative: Find, Show that, Hence (or Hence, or otherwise), Deduce, State, Sketch, Explain (why / whether / how you know / in context), Determine (whether / the possible values), Verify, Use … to …, Write down, Solve, Express, Describe (a sequence of transformations; the set of points; the relationship), Justify your answer, Give a reason, Suggest.
- Parts are (a), (b), (c) with sub-parts (i), (ii); every leaf part carries its marks in [ ]; a 3–6 mark question may be unparted. The parts of a long question BUILD: an early "Show that" prints the result the later parts need, and "Hence", "Using the result in part (b)" or "Use your answer to part (c)(i)" says so.
- Precision is stated when it matters: "giving your answer in exact form", "in the form a + ib where a and b are real numbers", "correct to 3 significant figures", "in terms of p", "to the nearest cent", "correct to 2 decimal places", "as a single simplified fraction"; otherwise the rubric's 3 s.f. applies and nothing is said. "Find exactly", "Find the exact value" and "Solve exactly" forbid a decimal; "Use calculus", "Using calculus", "By integration" and "Show by integration" forbid a calculator read-off; "Do not use a calculator in answering this question." opens a whole question (a complex-number question, an exact-integral question, an exact inequality); "Without using a calculator" opens a part. Section B says "State the distribution you use", "In this question you should state the parameters of any distributions you use", "Define any symbols you use", "Give your conclusion in the context of the question".
- The graphing calculator is assumed. Numerical roots, definite integrals, the regression constants, r, binomial and normal probabilities and inverse-normal values are READ from it and the question asks only for the value — a question that wants the working says so. Where a graph is used to find a solution the candidate sketches it. Unsupported calculator answers earn no method marks, so a 4-mark part is never a single calculator read.
- Notation is the syllabus's: \mathrm{f}: x \mapsto \frac{ax+k}{x-a}, x \in \mathbb{R}, x \neq a; \mathrm{f}(x), \mathrm{f}^{-1}, \mathrm{fg}, \mathrm{f}^2; \frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}, \frac{\mathrm{d}^2y}{\mathrm{d}x^2}, \int \ldots \,\mathrm{d}x; \sum_{r=1}^{n}; u_n and S_n; column vectors and \mathbf{i}, \mathbf{j}, \mathbf{k}; \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{a} + \lambda\mathbf{b}; \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n} = d; the cartesian line \frac{x+2}{3} = \frac{y-1}{2} = z - 5; z^{*}, |z|, \arg z; \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma^2), \mathrm{B}(n, p), \bar{X}, \mathrm{H}_0: \mu = 17.3, \mathrm{P}(A \mid B). Angles in radians unless degrees are named; \mathrm{e}^{x}, \ln x, \mathrm{i} upright.
- Contexts are brief, concrete and self-contained; they carry the numbers the model needs and nothing more (a pipeline under a river, an ornament cut from a sphere, a parachutist, a roller-coaster loop, savings then a loan, a company's two machines, a swimmer's times, a bird feeder, a quality-control sample). Units are given; constants are named ("where k is a positive constant", "where \alpha is a constant"). No story, no chattiness, no names beyond one or two.
- Paper 1 opens with 4–6-mark questions (a system of equations, an inequality, a vector fact, a complex-number question, a short sequence question) and climbs to two or three 12–15-mark closers — a differential-equation model, a vector problem in a stated 3-D situation, a finance question on arithmetic and geometric series, a parametric or graph model, a functions question with several parts — with one question that "may require concepts and skills from more than one topic" in a real-world context. Paper 2 Section A is four (occasionally five) pure questions of 6–13 marks; Section B climbs from a 5–6-mark probability or counting starter through binomial, normal, sampling and hypothesis-testing questions to a 12–17-mark closer, usually the regression or the normal-plus-test question, set in a real-world context.
- Section B asks for words as often as numbers: "State, in context, two assumptions needed for X to be well modelled by a binomial distribution", "Explain whether … should use a one-tailed or a two-tailed test", "State hypotheses for the test, defining any parameters you use", "give your conclusion in the context of the question", "Explain whether your estimate is reliable", "Explain what the scatter diagram tells you about the relationship", "Explain whether the 65 members comprise a sample or a population", "Explain why it is reasonable to assume that the two distributions are independent". A 1-mark explain part expects one sentence with the reason in it; a 2-mark one, two distinct points.
- Marks follow the work at about 1.8 minutes a mark (100 marks in 3 hours). 1–2 marks: state / write down / one deduction / one calculator value. 3–4: one standard routine, or a routine with one decision. 5–6: a routine with a decision and a second idea, a model built from the situation, or a proof. 7 or more in ONE part is rare and needs a chain (a differential equation solved from a substitution to a particular solution; a regression model chosen, fitted and used). Marks climb through each paper and through each section.

title: H2 Mathematics · Set 1 · Paper 2 · A-Level format

question.stem: A geometric series is given by $1 + \frac{x-1}{x+2} + \left(\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right)^{3} + \ldots$, where $x$ is real and $x \neq -2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the set of values of $x$ for which the series converges.
parts.answer: $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x > -\frac{1}{2}\right\}$

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the sum to infinity of the series, giving your answer as a single fraction in terms of $x$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find exactly the set of values of $x$ for which the sum to infinity of the series exceeds $\frac{2}{x}$.
parts.answer: $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -\frac{1}{2} < x < 0 \text{ or } x > \sqrt{7} - 1\right\}$

skills: §8 move 7 (two topics fused), with move 6 (the situation changes the maths): the convergence set $x > -\frac{1}{2}$ of a geometric series with ratio $\frac{x-1}{x+2}$ is the domain of a later inequality on its sum to infinity, unprinted in that part — the sign test gives $-1-\sqrt{7} < x < 0$ or $x > \sqrt{7}-1$, and convergence, not the sign test, cuts the first interval to $-\frac{1}{2} < x < 0$
convergence of a geometric series whose ratio is a rational function of $x$: $\left|\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right| < 1$ read as $|x-1| < |x+2|$ (nearer to $1$ than to $-2$), giving $x > -\frac{1}{2}$

noticing that the sum to infinity collapses to the linear $\frac{x+2}{3}$, defined for every $x$ though it is the sum only for $x > -\frac{1}{2}$, then solving $\frac{x+2}{3} > \frac{2}{x}$ exactly by a sign test on $\frac{x^2+2x-6}{3x}$ with the negative-$x$ interval kept (no cross-multiplying)
question.solution:
(a) The series is geometric with first term $1$ and common ratio $r = \frac{x-1}{x+2}$, so it converges if and only if $|r| < 1$.
$\left|\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right| < 1 \iff |x-1| < |x+2|$ (as $x \neq -2$).
Both sides are non-negative, so squaring keeps the inequality: $(x-1)^2 < (x+2)^2 \iff x^2 - 2x + 1 < x^2 + 4x + 4 \iff -6x < 3 \iff x > -\frac{1}{2}$.
(Equivalently: $x$ is nearer to $1$ than to $-2$ on the number line, so it lies to the right of their midpoint $-\frac{1}{2}$.)
The series converges for $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x > -\frac{1}{2}\right\}$. [M1 for $|x-1| < |x+2|$ or $-1 < \frac{x-1}{x+2} < 1$; A1]

(b) Sum to infinity $= \frac{1}{1 - r} = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{x-1}{x+2}} = \frac{x+2}{(x+2) - (x-1)} = \frac{x+2}{3}$. [B1]

(c) The decision: a sum to infinity exists only where the series converges, that is for $x > -\frac{1}{2}$ by part (a). The expression $\frac{x+2}{3}$ is defined for every $x$, but it is the sum of the series only on that set, so the inequality is solved on $x > -\frac{1}{2}$ and not on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
$\frac{x+2}{3} > \frac{2}{x} \iff \frac{x+2}{3} - \frac{2}{x} > 0 \iff \frac{x^2 + 2x - 6}{3x} > 0$. [M1: one side, single fraction, not cross-multiplied]
$x^2 + 2x - 6 = 0 \iff x = -1 \pm \sqrt{7}$, so the inequality is $\frac{\left(x + 1 + \sqrt{7}\right)\left(x + 1 - \sqrt{7}\right)}{3x} > 0$, with critical values $-1 - \sqrt{7}\ (\approx -3.65)$, $0$ and $\sqrt{7} - 1\ (\approx 1.65)$.
Sign test: for $x < -1 - \sqrt{7}$ the fraction is negative; for $-1 - \sqrt{7} < x < 0$ it is positive; for $0 < x < \sqrt{7} - 1$ it is negative; for $x > \sqrt{7} - 1$ it is positive.
So $\frac{x+2}{3} > \frac{2}{x} \iff -1 - \sqrt{7} < x < 0$ or $x > \sqrt{7} - 1$. [A1: the raw intervals from the sign test]
Restrict to $x > -\frac{1}{2}$: since $-1 - \sqrt{7} < -\frac{1}{2} < 0$, the first interval is cut to $-\frac{1}{2} < x < 0$; the second is unchanged because $\sqrt{7} - 1 > -\frac{1}{2}$. [M1: the inequality restricted to the convergence set $x > -\frac{1}{2}$, where alone $\frac{x+2}{3}$ is the sum]
Required set: $\left\{x \in \mathbb{R} : -\frac{1}{2} < x < 0 \text{ or } x > \sqrt{7} - 1\right\}$. [A1: the cut set. A candidate who solves $\frac{x+2}{3} > \frac{2}{x}$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$ scores M1 A1 M0 A0, 2 of the 4 marks]
The values $-1 - \sqrt{7} < x \le -\frac{1}{2}$ satisfy $\frac{x+2}{3} > \frac{2}{x}$ but are rejected: there $|r| \ge 1$ (for example $x = -1$ gives $r = -2$), so the series has no sum to infinity; that interval even contains $x = -2$, where the series is not defined.
Alternative (working on the convergence set from the start): for $-\frac{1}{2} < x < 0$ the sum $\frac{x+2}{3}$ lies between $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{2}{3}$, so it is positive while $\frac{2}{x} < 0$, and every such $x$ satisfies the inequality; for $x > 0$, multiplying by $3x > 0$ gives $x^2 + 2x - 6 > 0$, so $x > \sqrt{7} - 1$ (the other root, $-1 - \sqrt{7}$, is negative). The same set results.
Common errors: solving on all of $\mathbb{R}$ gives $-1 - \sqrt{7} < x < 0$ or $x > \sqrt{7} - 1$ (convergence forgotten, final A0); cross-multiplying by $x$ as though it were positive gives $x^2 + 2x - 6 > 0$ and loses the interval $-\frac{1}{2} < x < 0$.
Check: $x = -0.4$: $r = -0.875$, sum $= 0.533 > \frac{2}{-0.4} = -5$ (in the set); $x = 1.6$: sum $= 1.2 < 1.25$ (not in the set); $x = 1.7$: sum $= 1.233 > 1.176$ (in the set); $x = -1$: $\frac{x+2}{3} = \frac{1}{3} > -2$ but $r = -2$, no sum (rejected).
question.syllabus_check: 9758 Sequences and series: a geometric series, the condition $|r| < 1$ for convergence, and the sum to infinity. 9758 Equations and inequalities: a modulus inequality $|x - a| < |x - b|$, and an inequality $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} > 0$ with a quadratic numerator and a linear denominator solved by a sign test (never by cross-multiplying), with exact roots from the quadratic formula. No calculator ban (the Set's one ban question is in Paper 1); 'Find exactly' requires $\sqrt{7} - 1$, and the convergence step cannot be read from a calculator. Nothing outside the revised 9758: no method of differences, no induction, no polar form.
question.originality_note: No earlier Set has an Inequalities question. Set 1 P1 Q2(b) is a geometric series with a fixed ratio (first term 6, sum to infinity 4) and tests partial sums against the sum to infinity by the parity of $n$; here the ratio is a function of $x$, and the convergence set is the object. Among the real papers, GCE 2023 P2 Q1 and GCE 2024 P1 Q4 solve a rational inequality on all of $\mathbb{R}$, and GCE 2022 P1 Q9(b) sums a geometric series with ratio $-\cos\theta$ to a printed $\tan k\theta$; no 2017–2025 question makes the convergence set of a geometric series the domain of an inequality on its own sum. The sum collapses to the linear $\frac{x+2}{3}$, defined for every $x$, so nothing in part (c) reminds the candidate that the series has no sum for $x \le -\frac{1}{2}$ — and that set, not the sign test, fixes the left end of the answer. Implemented from the chosen idea (Q1.idea.md) with one change: the inequality is 'greater than $\frac{2}{x}$' rather than 'less than', so that the convergence boundary $-\frac{1}{2}$ is an endpoint of the final answer (the sign-test interval $-1-\sqrt{7} < x < 0$ is cut to $-\frac{1}{2} < x < 0$) instead of a whole interval merely discarded, and cross-multiplying is punished visibly; the planner's numbers ($\frac{x+2}{3}$, $-\frac{1}{2}$, $\sqrt{7} - 1$) are kept, and the sum in (b) is asked for, not printed as a 'Show that', so the collapse to a linear expression is the candidate's to notice. Nothing is shared with the first draft's Q1 ($|x - 4| < \frac{3}{x}$ carried into $\ln x$) or with any other slot of this paper.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give {x ∈ ℝ : x > −1/2}. Re-derived: |x−1| < |x+2|, both sides non-negative so squaring is safe, −6x < 3. Checked x = 0 (r = −1/2, converges) and x = −1 (r = −2, does not).

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give {x ∈ ℝ : −1/2 < x < 0 or x > √7 − 1}. Re-derived: (x+2)/3 − 2/x = (x² + 2x − 6)/(3x), critical values −1 ± √7 and 0; positive on (−1−√7, 0) ∪ (√7 − 1, ∞) (checked at x = −1 and x = −0.25: positive; x = 1.6: 1.2 < 1.25; x = 2: 4/3 > 1). The sum exists only on x > −1/2 (part (a)), which cuts the left interval to (−1/2, 0); the right interval is untouched. The setter's mark scheme, the common-error notes and the numerical checks are all correct.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on every part and I re-derived each one; the key is exactly right, including the cut of (−1−√7, 0) to (−1/2, 0) by the convergence set.
verdict.move: 7 Two topics fused (the GP's convergence set from (a) is the unprinted domain of the inequality on its sum in (c)), with 6 The situation changes the maths (the sum exists only where the series converges, so the sign-test interval (−1−√7, 0) is cut at −1/2 — an endpoint no sign test produces)
fixes: re-mark inside (c), totals unchanged at 2 + 1 + 4: pay the sign test M1 A1 (single fraction with critical values −1 ± √7 and 0; the raw intervals) and the restriction to the convergence set M1 A1 (recognising that (x+2)/3 is the sum only for x > −1/2; the cut set), so a candidate who solves (x+2)/3 > 2/x on all of ℝ scores 2/4 and not 3/4 — the decision is the question's point and at present carries one mark of seven, thinner than Set 1 P1 Q1(a) and Q2(b), where the decision carries most of the part.

Light wording edit to SEAB's register in (b): 'Find the sum to infinity of the series, giving your answer as a single fraction in terms of x.' (cf. GCE 2022 P2 Q4(b) 'Write your answer as a single fraction in terms of m') in place of 'in terms of x, simplifying your answer'.
verdict.why: The idea is implemented faithfully and a little better than briefed: (b) is a 'Find', not the sketched 'Show that', so the collapse to the linear (x+2)/3 must be noticed, and the '>' direction makes the convergence set supply an endpoint of the answer (−1/2) rather than merely delete an interval — the candidate must decide, unprompted in (c), that a formula defined for every x is the sum only on x > −1/2, and both wrong routes (solving on ℝ; cross-multiplying by x) leave a visibly different set. It scores 4 rather than 5 because the lead-in (a)–(b) is the familiar tutorial shape 'GP with ratio a rational function of x → convergence set → S∞(x)' and the decision carries one mark of seven, on a technical skeleton (a two-modulus inequality, then an exact rational inequality by sign test) that mirrors GCE 2023 P2 Q1 — a different object, an extra part and a different move, so not a re-skin, but the same techniques; no part asks for words (List A item 6), which the real 2022–2024 Section A openers also lack, so it is not held against an opener. Not routine: it is the paper's opener and carries a decision, so the routine allowance stays unused. question.stem: The curve $C$ has equation $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$, where $\mathrm{f}(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x}$ for $x > 0$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the exact coordinates of the stationary point of $C$, and show that it is a maximum point.
parts.answer: $\left(\mathrm{e}, \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}\right)$, a maximum: $\mathrm{f}'(x) = \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2}$ is positive for $0 < x < \mathrm{e}$ and negative for $x > \mathrm{e}$ (or $\mathrm{f}''(\mathrm{e}) = -\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^3} < 0$)

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Determine, with justification, which of $3^{\pi}$ and $\pi^{3}$ is greater.
parts.answer: $3^{\pi} > \pi^{3}$, since $3^{\pi} > \pi^{3} \iff \frac{\ln 3}{3} > \frac{\ln \pi}{\pi}$, i.e. $\mathrm{f}(3) > \mathrm{f}(\pi)$, which holds because $\mathrm{f}$ is decreasing for $x > \mathrm{e}$ and $\mathrm{e} < 3 < \pi$

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Show that $x^{\mathrm{e}} \leqslant \mathrm{e}^{x}$ for all $x > 0$.
parts.answer: Shown: $\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$ is the greatest value of $\mathrm{f}$, so $\frac{\ln x}{x} \leqslant \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$, giving $\mathrm{e}\ln x \leqslant x$, i.e. $\ln\left(x^{\mathrm{e}}\right) \leqslant \ln\left(\mathrm{e}^{x}\right)$, so $x^{\mathrm{e}} \leqslant \mathrm{e}^{x}$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Find, with justification, all the positive integers $n$ for which $n^{\frac{1}{n}} \geqslant \sqrt{2}$.
parts.answer: $n = 2, 3, 4$ (the inequality is $\mathrm{f}(n) \geqslant \mathrm{f}(2)$, and $\mathrm{f}(4) = \mathrm{f}(2)$ exactly since $\sqrt{2} = 4^{\frac{1}{4}}$; $\mathrm{f}(1) = 0$, and $\mathrm{f}$ decreases for $x > \mathrm{e}$ so $\mathrm{f}(n) < \mathrm{f}(4)$ for $n \geqslant 5$) — a candidate who gives the tie $\mathrm{f}(2) = \mathrm{f}(4)$ without excluding every $n \geqslant 5$ earns 1 of the 2 marks

skills: §8 move 10 (compare two claims algebraically): turning a comparison of powers $a^{b}$ against $b^{a}$ into $\frac{\ln a}{a}$ against $\frac{\ln b}{b}$ (take logarithms, divide by $ab$), so that $3^{\pi}$ against $\pi^{3}$ is decided by $\mathrm{f}$ DECREASING for $x > \mathrm{e}$ with $\mathrm{e} < 3 < \pi$ — a step the maximum alone cannot give
a global inequality from a single maximum: $\frac{\ln x}{x} \leqslant \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$ for all $x > 0$ rearranged to $x^{\mathrm{e}} \leqslant \mathrm{e}^{x}$

§8 move 4 (discrete reasoning): every positive integer $n$ with $n^{\frac{1}{n}} \geqslant \sqrt{2}$ from $\mathrm{f}(n) \geqslant \mathrm{f}(2)$, seeing $\sqrt{2} = 4^{\frac{1}{4}}$ exactly so that $\mathrm{f}(2) = \mathrm{f}(4)$, with the rise of $\mathrm{f}$ to $x = \mathrm{e}$ and its fall after it settling all $n$ (only $2, 3, 4$)
question.solution:
(a) By the quotient rule, $\mathrm{f}'(x) = \frac{x \cdot \frac{1}{x} - \ln x}{x^2} = \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2}$.
At a stationary point $\mathrm{f}'(x) = 0$, so $\ln x = 1$, giving $x = \mathrm{e}$ (the only solution), and $y = \frac{\ln \mathrm{e}}{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$. The stationary point is $\left(\mathrm{e}, \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}\right)$.
Nature: $x^2 > 0$, so $\mathrm{f}'(x)$ has the sign of $1 - \ln x$. For $0 < x < \mathrm{e}$, $\ln x < 1$ and $\mathrm{f}'(x) > 0$; for $x > \mathrm{e}$, $\ln x > 1$ and $\mathrm{f}'(x) < 0$. $\mathrm{f}'$ changes from positive to negative at $x = \mathrm{e}$, so the point is a maximum. (Or: $\mathrm{f}''(x) = \frac{2\ln x - 3}{x^3}$, and $\mathrm{f}''(\mathrm{e}) = -\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}^3} < 0$, so a maximum.)
[M1 quotient rule to $\frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2}$; A1 $\left(\mathrm{e}, \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}\right)$ exact; A1 maximum by a correct first- or second-derivative test.]

(b) Since $\ln$ is increasing, $3^{\pi} > \pi^{3} \iff \pi\ln 3 > 3\ln \pi \iff \frac{\ln 3}{3} > \frac{\ln \pi}{\pi}$ (dividing by $3\pi > 0$) $\iff \mathrm{f}(3) > \mathrm{f}(\pi)$.
From (a), $\mathrm{f}'(x) = \frac{1 - \ln x}{x^2} < 0$ for $x > \mathrm{e}$, so $\mathrm{f}$ is strictly decreasing for $x \geqslant \mathrm{e}$. Since $\mathrm{e} < 3 < \pi$, $\mathrm{f}(3) > \mathrm{f}(\pi)$.
Hence $3^{\pi} > \pi^{3}$.
[M1 the comparison of powers turned into $\mathrm{f}(3)$ against $\mathrm{f}(\pi)$ unprompted; M1 $\mathrm{f}$ decreasing for $x > \mathrm{e}$ with $\mathrm{e} < 3 < \pi$; A1 $3^{\pi} > \pi^{3}$. Calculator values ($3^{\pi} \approx 31.5$, $\pi^{3} \approx 31.0$) alone earn no marks. The maximum alone does not decide it (both 3 and $\pi$ lie beyond $\mathrm{e}$).]

(c) From (a), $\mathrm{f}$ increases for $0 < x < \mathrm{e}$ and decreases for $x > \mathrm{e}$, so $\frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$ is the greatest value of $\mathrm{f}$: $\frac{\ln x}{x} \leqslant \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$ for all $x > 0$.
Multiplying by $\mathrm{e}x$, which is positive: $\mathrm{e}\ln x \leqslant x$, that is, $\ln\left(x^{\mathrm{e}}\right) \leqslant x = \ln\left(\mathrm{e}^{x}\right)$.
Since $\ln$ is an increasing function, $x^{\mathrm{e}} \leqslant \mathrm{e}^{x}$ for all $x > 0$ (with equality only at $x = \mathrm{e}$).
[B1 $\frac{\ln x}{x} \leqslant \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}$ used as the greatest value of $\mathrm{f}$ for ALL $x > 0$ and rearranged through $\mathrm{e}\ln x \leqslant x$ to the printed result, the multiplier $\mathrm{e}x$ noted positive.]

(d) Since $\ln$ is increasing and $n > 0$, $n^{\frac{1}{n}} \geqslant \sqrt{2} = 2^{\frac{1}{2}} \iff \frac{1}{n}\ln n \geqslant \frac{1}{2}\ln 2 \iff \mathrm{f}(n) \geqslant \mathrm{f}(2)$.
Also $\sqrt{2} = \left(2^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{4}} = 4^{\frac{1}{4}}$, so $\mathrm{f}(4) = \frac{\ln 4}{4} = \frac{2\ln 2}{4} = \frac{\ln 2}{2} = \mathrm{f}(2)$ exactly.
$n = 1$: $\mathrm{f}(1) = 0 < \mathrm{f}(2)$, so $n = 1$ fails. $n = 2$: equality holds, so $n = 2$ satisfies the inequality.
For $n \geqslant 3$ we have $n > \mathrm{e}$, where $\mathrm{f}$ is strictly decreasing. $n = 3$: $3 < 4$ gives $\mathrm{f}(3) > \mathrm{f}(4) = \mathrm{f}(2)$, so $n = 3$ satisfies it. $n = 4$: equality, so $n = 4$ satisfies it. $n \geqslant 5$: $n > 4$ gives $\mathrm{f}(n) < \mathrm{f}(4) = \mathrm{f}(2)$, so every $n \geqslant 5$ fails.
Therefore $n = 2, 3, 4$ only.
[B1 the inequality as $\mathrm{f}(n) \geqslant \mathrm{f}(2)$ with $\mathrm{f}(4) = \mathrm{f}(2)$ seen exactly (from $\sqrt{2} = 4^{\frac{1}{4}}$); A1 $n = 2, 3, 4$ with every $n \geqslant 5$ excluded because $\mathrm{f}$ decreases for $x > \mathrm{e}$. A table of calculator values alone cannot settle all $n \geqslant 5$, nor the exact tie at $n = 4$ ($1.41421\ldots$ for both $n = 2$ and $n = 4$), and scores at most 1. A candidate who gives the tie $\mathrm{f}(2) = \mathrm{f}(4)$ without excluding every $n \geqslant 5$ earns 1 of the 2 marks.]

question.stem: The function $\mathrm{f}$ is defined by $\mathrm{f}: x \mapsto 1 - x^2,\ x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \geqslant 0$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ and state the domain of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$.
parts.answer: $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$; domain $x \leqslant 1$, i.e. $(-\infty, 1]$

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Sketch, on the same diagram, the graphs of $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$, showing clearly the relationship between the two graphs and stating the coordinates of the points where each graph meets the axes.
parts.answer: $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$: half-parabola from the end-point $(0, 1)$, decreasing through $(1, 0)$; $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$: its reflection in the line $y = x$, from the end-point $(1, 0)$ through $(0, 1)$, rising as $x \to -\infty$. Each graph meets the axes at $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the exact coordinates of the points at which the graphs of $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ meet, and show that there are no other such points.
parts.answer: $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $\left(\frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}\right)$ only: $1 - x^2 = \sqrt{1 - x}$ for $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$ gives $x(1 - x)(x^2 + x - 1) = 0$, and the fourth root $x = \frac{-1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}$ is rejected as it is not in $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The function $\mathrm{g}$ is increasing for all values of $x$ in its domain, so that $\mathrm{g}^{-1}$ exists. Explain why every point at which the graphs of $y = \mathrm{g}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{g}^{-1}(x)$ meet lies on the line $y = x$.
parts.answer: If $(a, b)$ is on both graphs, then $\mathrm{g}(a) = b$ and $\mathrm{g}(b) = a$. If $a < b$, g increasing gives $\mathrm{g}(a) < \mathrm{g}(b)$, i.e. $b < a$, a contradiction; similarly $a > b$ gives $b > a$. So $a = b$ and the point lies on $y = x$.

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: The function $\mathrm{h}$ is defined by $\mathrm{h}: x \mapsto 1 - x^2,\ x \in \mathbb{R},\ x \leqslant 0$. Use the result of part (d) to find the exact coordinates of the point at which the graphs of $y = \mathrm{h}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{h}^{-1}(x)$ meet.
parts.answer: $\left(-\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}, -\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$

question.answer: (a) $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$, domain $x \leqslant 1$; (b) $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ from the end-point $(0, 1)$ decreasing through $(1, 0)$, $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ its reflection in $y = x$ from the end-point $(1, 0)$ through $(0, 1)$; (c) $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $\left(\frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}\right)$, and no others; (d) $\mathrm{g}(a) = b$ and $\mathrm{g}(b) = a$ with $a \neq b$ contradicts g increasing, so $a = b$; (e) $\left(-\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}, -\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\right)$
skills: §8 move 5 (show which, and that there are no others): finding ALL the meeting points of $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ for a DECREASING $\mathrm{f}$ by solving $\mathrm{f}(x) = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ itself (or $\mathrm{f}^2(x) = x$), not the habitual $\mathrm{f}(x) = x$ — the count is not printed; the squared equation factorises as $x(1 - x)(x^2 + x - 1) = 0$, giving the reflected pair $(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ off the line $y = x$ beside $\left(\frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}\right)$, with the root outside $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$ rejected

§8 move 12 (geometry seen, not computed): the sketch of $\mathrm{f}$ and $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ sharing both intercepts $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ read as the sign that a decreasing function meets its reflection away from the mirror line ($\mathrm{f}(0) = 1$ and $\mathrm{f}(1) = 0$ swap)

§8 move 9 (a reasoning-only part): proving that for an INCREASING $\mathrm{g}$ every meeting point of $y = \mathrm{g}(x)$ and $y = \mathrm{g}^{-1}(x)$ lies on $y = x$ ($\mathrm{g}(a) = b$, $\mathrm{g}(b) = a$ with $a \neq b$ contradicts monotonicity), then using it on the increasing branch $x \leqslant 0$ of $1 - x^2$, whose single meeting point is the root rejected in (c)
question.solution:
(a) Let $y = 1 - x^2$, $x \geqslant 0$. Then $x^2 = 1 - y$, and $x = \sqrt{1 - y}$, taking the positive square root because $x \geqslant 0$.
So $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$.
f is decreasing for $x \geqslant 0$, with $\mathrm{f}(0) = 1$ and $\mathrm{f}(x) \to -\infty$ as $x \to \infty$, so $R_{\mathrm{f}} = (-\infty, 1]$.
$D_{\mathrm{f}^{-1}} = R_{\mathrm{f}} = (-\infty, 1]$, i.e. $x \leqslant 1$.
[B1 $\sqrt{1 - x}$, the positive root; B1 the domain.]

(b) One diagram, equal scales, the line $y = x$ drawn (dashed) as the mirror line.
$y = \mathrm{f}(x)$: the right half of the parabola $y = 1 - x^2$, starting at the end-point $(0, 1)$ on the $y$-axis (horizontal tangent there), decreasing and concave downwards, crossing the $x$-axis at $(1, 0)$ and continuing downwards as $x$ increases.
$y = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{1 - x}$: the reflection of $y = \mathrm{f}(x)$ in the line $y = x$, starting at the end-point $(1, 0)$ on the $x$-axis (vertical tangent there), crossing the $y$-axis at $(0, 1)$ and rising as $x \to -\infty$.
Each graph meets the axes at $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$, so the two graphs share both of these points; between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ the graph of $\mathrm{f}$ is first above that of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ and then below it, crossing it on the line $y = x$.
[B1 each curve with its end-point and its intercepts; B1 the two graphs clearly reflections of each other in $y = x$.]

(c) A point $(p, q)$ lies on both graphs when $q = \mathrm{f}(p)$ and $q = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(p)$, with $p$ in both domains: $p \geqslant 0$ and $p \leqslant 1$.
Solving $\mathrm{f}(x) = x$ finds only the meeting points ON the line $y = x$. Here $\mathrm{f}$ is decreasing, and the sketch in (b) already shows two common points off that line, so the equation to solve is $\mathrm{f}(x) = \mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$ itself:
$1 - x^2 = \sqrt{1 - x}$, $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$.
For $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$ both sides are non-negative, so squaring gives an equivalent equation:
$(1 - x^2)^2 = 1 - x$
$(1 - x)^2(1 + x)^2 - (1 - x) = 0$
$(1 - x)\left[(1 - x)(1 + x)^2 - 1\right] = 0$
$(1 - x)(1 + x - x^2 - x^3 - 1) = 0$
$(1 - x)(x - x^2 - x^3) = 0$
$x(1 - x)(1 - x - x^2) = 0$.
[Alternatively: $(p, q)$ is on the graph of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$ exactly when $\mathrm{f}(q) = p$, so a common point has $\mathrm{f}(\mathrm{f}(p)) = p$: $1 - (1 - x^2)^2 = x$, i.e. $x^4 - 2x^2 + x = 0$, $x(x - 1)(x^2 + x - 1) = 0$ — the same equation. The sketch shows that $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ are roots, which gives the factor $x(x - 1)$ at once.]
So $x = 0$, $x = 1$, or $x^2 + x - 1 = 0$, giving $x = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{5}}{2}$.
$x = \frac{-1 - \sqrt{5}}{2} \approx -1.62$ is not in $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$ (it is outside the domain of $\mathrm{f}$): rejected. [There $1 - x^2 < 0 < \sqrt{1 - x}$, so it came only from squaring.]
$x = \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2} \approx 0.618$ lies in $0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$.
$y$-coordinates: $\mathrm{f}(0) = 1$; $\mathrm{f}(1) = 0$; for $x = \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$, $x^2 = 1 - x$, so $\mathrm{f}(x) = 1 - x^2 = x = \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}$.
The quartic has only these four roots and one of them is rejected, so the graphs meet at exactly three points:
$(0, 1)$, $(1, 0)$ and $\left(\frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}, \frac{\sqrt{5} - 1}{2}\right)$.
Two of them lie off the line $y = x$: $\mathrm{f}(0) = 1$ and $\mathrm{f}(1) = 0$, so $(0, 1)$ and $(1, 0)$ are both on the graph of $\mathrm{f}$, and as each is the reflection of the other in $y = x$, both are also on the graph of $\mathrm{f}^{-1}$.
[M1 equating $\mathrm{f}(x)$ and $\mathrm{f}^{-1}(x)$, or $\mathrm{f}^2(x) = x$ — NOT $\mathrm{f}(x) = x$; M1 squaring and factorising the quartic; A1 the four roots with $\frac{-1 - \sqrt{5}}{2}$ rejected for a stated reason; A1 all three points exact. A candidate who solves only $\mathrm{f}(x) = x$ earns at most 1 mark.]

(d) Let $(a, b)$ be a point on both graphs. Then $b = \mathrm{g}(a)$, and $b = \mathrm{g}^{-1}(a)$ gives $\mathrm{g}(b) = a$.
Suppose $a < b$. Since $\mathrm{g}$ is increasing, $\mathrm{g}(a) < \mathrm{g}(b)$, that is $b < a$ — a contradiction.
Suppose $a > b$. Then $\mathrm{g}(a) > \mathrm{g}(b)$, that is $b > a$ — a contradiction.
Hence $a = b$, and the point $(a, b)$ lies on the line $y = x$.
[For the decreasing $\mathrm{f}$ of part (c), $a < b$ gives $\mathrm{f}(a) > \mathrm{f}(b)$, that is $b > a$, which is no contradiction — which is why a point such as $(0, 1)$, with $a = 0$ and $b = 1$, can occur.]
[B1 $\mathrm{g}(a) = b$ and $\mathrm{g}(b) = a$; B1 the contradiction from $\mathrm{g}$ increasing, in both cases or 'without loss of generality'.]

question.stem: The inside of a vase has a flat horizontal base and an open top at a height of $2\pi$ cm above the base. At height $y$ cm above the base, where $0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2\pi$, the horizontal cross-section of the inside of the vase is a circle of radius $(3 + \cos y)$ cm (see diagram). The vase is initially empty and water is poured into it at a constant rate of $12\pi$ cm$^3$ per second; at time $t$ seconds after pouring begins, the depth of the water is $h$ cm.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the rate at which the depth of the water is increasing at the instant when $h = \frac{1}{2}\pi$. Find also the rate of change of the radius of the water surface at this instant.
parts.answer: The depth is increasing at $\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second. The rate of change of the radius of the water surface is $-\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second: the radius is decreasing at $\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the exact time taken to fill the vase.
parts.answer: $\frac{19\pi}{12}$ seconds (the capacity is $19\pi^2$ cm$^3$)

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the exact depth of the water at the instant when half of the time found in part (b) has passed. Justify your answer.
parts.answer: $\pi$ cm. The rate of flow is constant, so the vase then holds half its capacity; since $3 + \cos(2\pi - y) = 3 + \cos y$, the vase is symmetric about its narrowest section at $y = \pi$, so exactly half the capacity lies below $y = \pi$, and $V$ increases with $h$, so this is the only such depth.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Without further differentiation, find the greatest and least values of the rate at which the depth of the water increases for $0 \leqslant h \leqslant 2\pi$, and state the depths of the water at which they occur.
parts.answer: Greatest $3$ cm per second, when $h = \pi$ (the narrowest section); least $\frac{3}{4}$ cm per second, when $h = 0$ and when $h = 2\pi$ (the widest sections).

question.answer: (a) Depth increasing at $\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second; radius of the water surface changing at $-\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second (decreasing). (b) $\frac{19\pi}{12}$ s. (c) $\pi$ cm (half the capacity, and the vase is symmetric about its narrowest section $y = \pi$). (d) Greatest $3$ cm per second at $h = \pi$; least $\frac{3}{4}$ cm per second at $h = 0$ and $h = 2\pi$.
skills: §8 move 12 (geometry seen, not computed): with no formula for the volume printed, seeing that $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}h}$ is the area of the water surface, $\pi(3 + \cos h)^2$ (a thin horizontal layer, or $V = \int_0^h \pi(3 + \cos y)^2\,\mathrm{d}y$), so the chain rule gives $\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{12}{(3 + \cos h)^2}$; then a second chain through the surface radius $r = 3 + \cos h$, which is DECREASING ($-\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second at $h = \frac{1}{2}\pi$) while the water rises, because the vase narrows

§8 move 2 (reverse the direction) (a time given, the depth asked), with a reasoning-only part (move 9): the depth after half the fill time read from the vase's symmetry about its narrowest section (constant inflow gives half the volume; $\cos(2\pi - y) = \cos y$) as exactly $\pi$, instead of solving the transcendental $V(h) = \frac{1}{2}V(2\pi)$; the greatest and least rates of rise, $3$ and $\frac{3}{4}$ cm per second at the narrowest and widest sections, read from $\frac{12}{(3 + \cos h)^2}$ without differentiating again
question.figure_description: A vertical cross-section of the vase through its axis of symmetry (a flat 2-D drawing, not a 3-D view), same scale on both directions, drawing window: horizontal from -5 to 5, vertical from -0.5 to 7 (in cm). No coordinate axes, gridlines, tick marks or equations are drawn. The axis of symmetry is a vertical dashed line through the middle. The inside wall of the vase is two smooth curves that are mirror images of each other in the axis: on the right, the curve whose horizontal distance from the axis at height y is 3 + cos y for 0 <= y <= 2pi (distance 4 at the base, narrowing smoothly to 2 at y = pi, widening again to 4 at y = 2pi, about 6.28 high), and its reflection on the left. (The formula and the height y = pi of the narrowest point are drawing instructions only: neither is printed on the figure.) A thin outer wall may be drawn a small constant distance outside each curve. The base is a horizontal straight line joining the two curves at height 0 (width 8); the top at height 2pi is open (no line across it). Water is shaded lightly from the base up to a level surface at a height of about 1.2 (below the narrowest point), the water surface drawn as a horizontal line between the two curves. Labels: a double-headed vertical arrow outside the vase on the right, from the base to the water surface, labelled 'h cm'; a double-headed vertical arrow outside the vase on the left, from the base to the open top, labelled '2π cm'; three horizontal single-headed arrows from the axis to the right-hand wall, at the base labelled '4 cm', at the narrowest point labelled '2 cm', and at the top labelled '4 cm'. Nothing else is labelled: no height of the narrowest point, no formula 3 + cos y, no radius of the water surface, no volume, no rate, no time.
question.solution:
(a) Let the radius of the water surface be $r$ cm, so $r = 3 + \cos h$.
No formula for the volume $V$ cm$^3$ of water is given. The water is made of thin horizontal circular slices: the volume of water is $V = \int_0^h \pi(3 + \cos y)^2\,\mathrm{d}y$ (the region between the curve $x = 3 + \cos y$ and the $y$-axis, for $0 \leqslant y \leqslant h$, rotated about the $y$-axis). Raising the depth by a small $\delta h$ adds a thin layer of volume $\delta V \approx \pi(3 + \cos h)^2\,\delta h$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}h} = \pi(3 + \cos h)^2$, the area of the water surface. [B1]
(Or integrate first: $V = \pi\int_0^h \left(9 + 6\cos y + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos 2y\right)\mathrm{d}y = \pi\left(\frac{19}{2}h + 6\sin h + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2h\right)$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}h} = \pi\left(\frac{19}{2} + 6\cos h + \frac{1}{2}\cos 2h\right) = \pi(9 + 6\cos h + \cos^2 h) = \pi(3 + \cos h)^2$.)
$\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t} \div \frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}h} = \frac{12\pi}{\pi(3 + \cos h)^2} = \frac{12}{(3 + \cos h)^2}$. [M1]
When $h = \frac{1}{2}\pi$, $\cos h = 0$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{12}{9} = \frac{4}{3}$: the depth is increasing at $\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second. [A1]
$\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}h} \times \frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\sin h \times \frac{12}{(3 + \cos h)^2}$. [M1]
When $h = \frac{1}{2}\pi$, $\sin h = 1$, so $\frac{\mathrm{d}r}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\frac{4}{3}$: the radius of the water surface is DECREASING at $\frac{4}{3}$ cm per second (for $0 < h < \pi$ the vase narrows as the water rises). [A1] (The answer $+\frac{4}{3}$, or 'increasing', earns A0.)

(b) The vase is full when $h = 2\pi$. Its capacity is
$\int_0^{2\pi} \pi(3 + \cos y)^2\,\mathrm{d}y = \pi\int_0^{2\pi} \left(9 + 6\cos y + \cos^2 y\right)\mathrm{d}y$ [M1]
$= \pi\int_0^{2\pi} \left(9 + 6\cos y + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos 2y\right)\mathrm{d}y$, using $\cos^2 y = \frac{1}{2}(1 + \cos 2y)$ [M1]
$= \pi\left[\frac{19}{2}y + 6\sin y + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2y\right]_0^{2\pi} = \pi(19\pi + 0 + 0) = 19\pi^2$ cm$^3$. [A1]
(Over the full period $0 \leqslant y \leqslant 2\pi$ the $\cos y$ term contributes nothing and $\cos^2 y$ contributes $\pi$.)
Time taken $= \frac{19\pi^2}{12\pi} = \frac{19\pi}{12}$ seconds ($\approx 4.97$ s). [A1]
(A calculator value alone, $187.5$ cm$^3$ or $4.97$ s, is not exact and earns only the first M1 if the integral is set up.)

(c) Water enters at a constant rate, so when half of $\frac{19\pi}{12}$ s, that is $\frac{19\pi}{24}$ s, has passed, the vase holds half its capacity, $\frac{19\pi^2}{2}$ cm$^3$. [B1]
The radius at height $2\pi - y$ is $3 + \cos(2\pi - y) = 3 + \cos y$, the radius at height $y$: the inside of the vase is symmetric about the horizontal plane at height $\pi$, its narrowest section (radius 2). So the part of the vase below height $\pi$ holds exactly half the capacity, and since $V$ increases as $h$ increases, no other depth gives half: the depth is $\pi$ cm. [B1]
(Check with $V$ from (a): $V = \pi\left(\frac{19}{2}\pi + 6\sin \pi + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2\pi\right) = \frac{19\pi^2}{2}$ when $h = \pi$. A calculator solution of $\frac{19}{2}h + 6\sin h + \frac{1}{4}\sin 2h = \frac{19}{2}\pi$ giving $3.14$ earns the second mark only when the exact value $\pi$ is stated and verified.)

(d) From (a), $\frac{\mathrm{d}h}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{12}{(3 + \cos h)^2}$: the depth rises fastest where the water surface is smallest and slowest where it is largest. Since $-1 \leqslant \cos h \leqslant 1$, $2 \leqslant 3 + \cos h \leqslant 4$.
Greatest rate $= \frac{12}{2^2} = 3$ cm per second, when $\cos h = -1$, that is $h = \pi$ (the narrowest section). [B1]
Least rate $= \frac{12}{4^2} = \frac{3}{4}$ cm per second, when $\cos h = 1$, that is $h = 0$ (as pouring begins) and $h = 2\pi$ (as the vase becomes full). [B1]
(The greatest rate is 4 times the least: $\left(\frac{4}{2}\right)^2$, the ratio of the areas of the widest and narrowest sections. By (c), the depth rises fastest exactly half way through the filling, when $t = \frac{19\pi}{24}$.)

question.stem: The integers $1$, $2$, $3$, $4$ and $5$ are arranged in a row, each integer being used exactly once. Such an arrangement is called a 'ridge' if the integers to the left of $5$ increase from left to right and the integers to the right of $5$ decrease from left to right. For example, $2 \quad 3 \quad 5 \quad 4 \quad 1$ and $5 \quad 4 \quad 3 \quad 2 \quad 1$ are ridges, but $2 \quad 5 \quad 3 \quad 4 \quad 1$ is not.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the number of ridges in which $5$ is in the middle position.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Show that there are $16$ ridges.
parts.answer: Shown: each of $1, 2, 3, 4$ is either to the left or to the right of $5$, giving $2^4 = 16$ choices, and each choice gives exactly one ridge because the order on each side is then forced (or ${}^4C_0 + {}^4C_1 + {}^4C_2 + {}^4C_3 + {}^4C_4 = 16$).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Explain why, in every ridge, $1$ is at one of the two ends.
parts.answer: $1$ is the smallest integer: if it is to the left of $5$ it must come first, since the integers there increase from the left-hand end; if it is to the right of $5$ it must come last, since the integers there decrease to the right-hand end.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: The integers $1, 2, 3, \ldots, n$, where $n \geqslant 2$, are now arranged in a row in a random order, and a ridge is defined in the same way, with $n$ in place of $5$. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which the probability that the arrangement is a ridge is less than $0.01$.

question.answer: (a) $6$; (b) $16$ (shown); (c) $1$ is the smallest integer, so it is first if it is on the increasing side and last if it is on the decreasing side; (d) $n = 8$
skills: §8 move 1 (define, then reason): seeing that a 'ridge' defined in the question is fixed by WHICH integers lie to the left of the largest (their order is then forced), so ridges are counted as subsets, ${}^4C_2$ with $5$ in the middle and $2^{n-1}$ in all, not as arrangements
structural reasoning from a definition: the smallest integer must stand at an end of every ridge (first on the increasing side, last on the decreasing side)

carrying the count to general $n$ unprompted and finding the smallest $n$ for which the probability $\frac{2^{n-1}}{n!}$ that a random arrangement is a ridge falls below $0.01$ (a table of values on the calculator earns full marks)
question.solution:
(a) With $5$ in the middle position there are two integers on each side of it. Choose which $2$ of $1, 2, 3, 4$ go to the left of $5$: ${}^4C_2 = 6$ ways. The two on the left must be written in increasing order and the two on the right in decreasing order, so each choice gives exactly one ridge.
Number of ridges $= 6$.

(b) In a ridge, each of the integers $1, 2, 3, 4$ is either to the left or to the right of $5$: $2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 = 2^4$ ways of splitting them into the two sides. Once the two sides are decided, the integers on the left must be in increasing order and those on the right in decreasing order, so each split gives exactly one ridge, and different splits give different ridges.
Number of ridges $= 2^4 = 16$ (shown).
[Alternatively, with $k$ integers to the left of $5$ ($k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4$) there are ${}^4C_k$ ridges, as in (a), so the total is ${}^4C_0 + {}^4C_1 + {}^4C_2 + {}^4C_3 + {}^4C_4 = 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16$.]

(c) $1$ is not $5$, so it is on one side of $5$, and it is the smallest of the integers. If $1$ is to the left of $5$: the integers there increase from left to right, so the smallest of them is first, and $1$ is at the left-hand end. If $1$ is to the right of $5$: the integers there decrease from left to right, so the smallest of them is last, and $1$ is at the right-hand end. Either way $1$ is at one of the two ends.

(d) As in (b), each of $1, 2, \ldots, n-1$ is either to the left or to the right of $n$, and the order on each side is then forced, so there are $2^{n-1}$ ridges.
[Alternatively, by (c): removing $1$ from a ridge of $1, 2, \ldots, n$ leaves a ridge of $2, 3, \ldots, n$, and $1$ can be placed at either end of any such ridge, so the number of ridges doubles each time $n$ increases by $1$; with $1$ ridge when $n = 1$, there are $2^{n-1}$.]
There are $n!$ equally likely arrangements, so
$\mathrm{P}(\text{ridge}) = p_n = \frac{2^{n-1}}{n!}$.
$\frac{p_{n+1}}{p_n} = \frac{2^{n}}{(n+1)!} \times \frac{n!}{2^{n-1}} = \frac{2}{n+1} < 1$ for $n \geqslant 2$, so $p_n$ decreases as $n$ increases.
$p_6 = \frac{32}{720} = 0.0444$
$p_7 = \frac{64}{5040} = 0.0127 > 0.01$
$p_8 = \frac{128}{40320} = 0.00317 < 0.01$
Smallest value of $n$ is $8$.

question.stem: A lamp is controlled by a worn push-button switch. Each time the switch is pressed, the lamp changes state (from on to off, or from off to on) with probability $p$, where $0 < p < 1$, and otherwise stays as it is, independently of what happens at any other press. The lamp is on before the switch is first pressed, and the probability that the lamp is on after the switch has been pressed $n$ times is denoted by $L_n$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Show that $L_n = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^n\right]$.
parts.answer: $L_n = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^n\right]$ (shown): the lamp is on exactly when the number of presses that change its state, $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$, is even, and adding the expansions of $(q + p)^n$ and $(q - p)^n$, where $q = 1 - p$, gives $2\,\mathrm{P}(X \text{ even}) = 1 + (1 - 2p)^n$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Without using the result in part (a), explain why $L_n = \frac{1}{2}$ for every positive integer $n$ when $p = \frac{1}{2}$.
parts.answer: Whatever the state of the lamp just before the last press, that press changes the state with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and leaves it unchanged with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, so after it the lamp is on with probability $\frac{1}{2}$; the earlier presses make no difference.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: For a particular switch, $p = 0.9$. Find $L_{10}$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: For a different switch, $L_2 = 0.58$. Find the possible values of $p$.
parts.answer: $p = 0.3$ or $p = 0.7$ (both kept: $\frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^2\right] = 0.58$ gives $(1 - 2p)^2 = 0.16$, $1 - 2p = \pm 0.4$, and both values lie in $0 < p < 1$; a candidate who rejects one of them loses the A mark)

parts.label: (e)
parts.text: For any switch, explain, in context, what happens to $L_n$ as $n$ becomes large.
parts.answer: $L_n \to \frac{1}{2}$, since $|1 - 2p| < 1$ so $(1 - 2p)^n \to 0$: after many presses the lamp is almost equally likely to be on or off, whatever the value of $p$, so the fact that it started on no longer matters.

question.solution:
(a) Let $X$ be the number of the $n$ presses that change the state of the lamp. The $n$ presses are independent and each changes the state with the same probability $p$, so $X \sim \mathrm{B}(n, p)$. Every change of state switches the lamp between on and off, and the lamp starts on, so after $n$ presses the lamp is on exactly when it has changed state an even number of times, that is, when $X$ is even. [B1]
Hence, with $q = 1 - p$, $L_n = \mathrm{P}(X \text{ even}) = \sum_{k \text{ even}} \binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k}$.
By the binomial theorem,
$(q + p)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} p^k q^{n-k} = \mathrm{P}(X \text{ even}) + \mathrm{P}(X \text{ odd})$,
$(q - p)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} (-p)^k q^{n-k} = \mathrm{P}(X \text{ even}) - \mathrm{P}(X \text{ odd})$, since $(-p)^k = p^k$ when $k$ is even and $(-p)^k = -p^k$ when $k$ is odd. [M1]
Adding, with $q + p = 1$ and $q - p = 1 - 2p$: $1 + (1 - 2p)^n = 2\,\mathrm{P}(X \text{ even})$, so $L_n = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^n\right]$. [A1]
Alternative route (full marks): conditioning on the state just before the $(n+1)$th press, $L_{n+1} = (1 - p)L_n + p(1 - L_n) = p + (1 - 2p)L_n$ [B1]. Then $L_{n+1} - \frac{1}{2} = (1 - 2p)\left(L_n - \frac{1}{2}\right)$, so $L_n - \frac{1}{2}$ is a geometric sequence with common ratio $1 - 2p$ [M1]; since $L_1 = 1 - p$ gives $L_1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - 2p)$, $L_n - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}(1 - 2p)^n$ and $L_n = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^n\right]$ [A1].
Check: $L_1 = 1 - p = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)\right]$ and $L_2 = (1 - p)^2 + p^2 = 1 - 2p + 2p^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^2\right]$. Verifying the formula for particular values of $n$ only does not show it.

(b) Consider the last ($n$th) press. Whatever the state of the lamp just before it, this press changes the state with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and leaves it unchanged with probability $\frac{1}{2}$, so $L_n = \frac{1}{2}L_{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}(1 - L_{n-1}) = \frac{1}{2}$ for every $n \geqslant 1$: the last press alone decides whether the lamp is on, and the earlier presses make no difference. [B1] (Consistent with part (a): $p = \frac{1}{2}$ makes $(1 - 2p)^n = 0$.)

(c) With $p = 0.9$, $1 - 2p = -0.8$, so $L_{10} = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (-0.8)^{10}\right] = \frac{1}{2}(1 + 0.107374) = 0.553687 = 0.554$ (3 s.f.). [B1]

(d) $L_2 = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + (1 - 2p)^2\right] = 0.58$, so $(1 - 2p)^2 = 0.16$ and $1 - 2p = 0.4$ or $1 - 2p = -0.4$. [M1: the formula at $n = 2$ solved for $(1 - 2p)^2$, both square roots taken]
So $p = 0.3$ or $p = 0.7$. Both values lie in $0 < p < 1$, so both are possible: a switch that changes the state with probability $0.3$ and one that changes it with probability $0.7$ give the same $L_2$ (check: $0.7^2 + 0.3^2 = 0.58$ either way), because after an even number of presses the two switches cannot be told apart. [A1: both values; rejecting one of them earns A0]

(e) For $0 < p < 1$, $-1 < 1 - 2p < 1$, so $(1 - 2p)^n \to 0$ and $L_n \to \frac{1}{2}$ as $n \to \infty$. In context: after a large number of presses the lamp is almost equally likely to be on or off, whatever the value of $p$ — the fact that it started on no longer affects its state. [B1] (For $p = 0.9$ the values of $L_n$ lie alternately above and below $\frac{1}{2}$ and close in on $\frac{1}{2}$; for $p < \frac{1}{2}$ they decrease towards $\frac{1}{2}$ from above.)
